cards.text: Hosea the prophet keeps bringing the LORD's message to Israel, and now he turns to Ephraim. Once upon a time, when Ephraim spoke, people TREMBLED. He was exalted in Israel, the one who talked and the whole room went quiet.

cards.question: Ephraim was exalted in Israel. But then he incurred guilt, and he died. What did Ephraim incur guilt through?

cards.text: And it doesn't stop there. Now they sin more and more, turning their own silver into cast images, idols skillfully made by craftsmen. FIVE-STAR craftsmanship. Zero-star idea.

cards.question: People talk about the ones making these silver idols. True or false: people say they kiss the calves.

cards.text: So where does chasing idols get them? Next come four quick pictures of what they'll be like.

cards.question: They'll be like the morning mist, like early dew, like chaff blown from a threshing floor, and like smoke through an open window. What do all four pictures have in common?

cards.text: Then the LORD speaks: "Yet I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt; you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me."

cards.question: The LORD goes way back with His people, all the way to Egypt. He says, "I knew you in the ___, in the land of drought."

cards.text: Then they finally get pasture, and when they have pasture, they're satisfied. Full, comfy, feet up.

cards.question: Once the people are satisfied in their pasture, their hearts become proud. What happens as a result?

cards.text: Pray hard for the job, get the job, and the praying stops on payday. Here, the LORD answers with wild animals: He'll be like a lion pouncing, like a leopard lurking by the path, like a wild beast tearing them apart.

cards.question: One more animal joins the lion and the leopard, and she's the fiercest of all: "Like a ___ robbed of her cubs I will attack them."

cards.text: After all those wild animals, the LORD drops the pictures and talks straight to Israel. No pictures this time. Just the truth, and it lands harder than a rolling pin off the top shelf.

cards.question: The LORD tells Israel they are destroyed. Why does He say it happened?

answers.text: Their king lost a great battle

cards.text: Then the LORD asks where their king is now to save them, after they said, "Give me a king and princes." It's like hiring the guy who swore he'd fix everything, and the night the storm hits, he's not picking up.

cards.question: The LORD talks about the king Israel asked for. True or false: the LORD says He gave Israel a king as a reward.

cards.text: In His anger He gave them a king, and in His wrath He took him away. And Ephraim's sin is bound up and stored up, the one box in the whole bakery I would NEVER want to open.

cards.question: Then Ephraim is pictured as a baby about to be born. Labor pains come and the time arrives, but he is an unwise son. What does Ephraim do?

answers.text: He stays put and won't come out
He comes out before the pains
He comes out grabbing a heel

cards.text: Then, right in the middle of all this, the LORD says, "I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death." And He calls out, "Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?"

cards.question: The LORD says He will ransom His people from Sheol and asks Death where its plagues and sting are. What do those questions show about Death?

answers.text: It is no match for the LORD
It always gets the final word

cards.text: But the verse ends, "Compassion is hidden from My eyes." Ephraim may be flourishing among his brothers, but a wind is coming.

cards.question: An east wind is coming against Ephraim, "a wind from the ___ rising up from the desert."
True or false: when the east wind comes, Ephraim's spring keeps on flowing.

cards.text: His fountain fails, his spring runs dry, and the wind plunders his treasury of every precious article. Then the message turns to Samaria, a city of Israel (1 Kings 16:24).

cards.question: Samaria will bear her guilt. Why?

cards.text: And the cost is terrible. They will fall by the sword, and even the little ones and the pregnant women will not be spared.

findings.problem: Ephraim appears for the first time and is never introduced. The card does not say who or what Ephraim is (Israel's northern kingdom, named for its leading tribe). "Now he turns to Ephraim" also suggests a new subject, but the chapter before this passage is already about Ephraim (Hosea 12:1, 8, 14).

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The saying in Hosea 13:2 is "They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!" The walkthrough only covers kissing the calves. Human sacrifice, the darkest detail of the verse, is never told anywhere.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The text says "People say of them," which does not make clear whether "them" means the idol makers or the idols. The card settles it as "the ones making these silver idols."

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question calls the bear "the fiercest of all." Hosea 13:7-8 never ranks the animals, so this claim is not in the text.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The question already says "Labor pains come and the time arrives." That rules out the wrong answer "He comes out before the pains."

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer "He stays put and won't come out" makes it sound like a refusal. The text says he "fails to present himself at the opening of the womb."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question gives one reading of Death's questions ("It is no match for the LORD") as the meaning. The next line, "Compassion is hidden from My eyes," and the judgment in 13:15-16 leave room for other readings. Because of that, a baker could argue for the wrong answer "It always gets the final word."

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: In the context of 13:14-16, a baker could argue that the wrong answer "It always gets the final word" is right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The question gives away the answer by ruling out both wrong answers. It says "An east wind," which rules out "north," and "rising up from the desert," which rules out "sea." It also asks the baker to fill in the wording of the line, not its meaning.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.
